title: The role that can do anything
brief: 18:20. A reporting job needs to read one bucket. It was given a role with a wildcard, because that was quicker. Its credential has just turned up in a log.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The job needs to read one bucket. If its credential leaks, the attacker gets the whole account.
teaches: Grant the smallest set of actions on the smallest set of resources
Use short lived role credentials, not long lived keys
Measure what a role really uses, and trim the rest

value.title: IAM console: role report-service
value.intro: Pretend the leaked credential is yours. See what it can do, beyond running a report.

attempts.label: List every database in the account
attempts.response:
3 databases: customers-prod, payments-prod, hr-prod

The report job can see them all.
attempts.fixedResponse: AccessDenied: report-service is not allowed to list databases

attempts.label: Delete the backups
attempts.response:
Deleted 41 backups.

The same credential can destroy the recovery copies.
attempts.fixedResponse: AccessDenied: report-service is not allowed to delete backups

fix.step: Pick the fix that closes the hole
fix.prompt: Pick every change that cuts the role down to what it needs, and limits how long a leaked credential is useful.

options.label: Allow only reading the reports bucket
options.why: The role can do its job and nothing else. A leaked credential can read reports.

options.label: Use short lived role credentials instead of a long lived key
options.why: A credential in a log stops working in an hour, instead of working for years.

options.label: Review access reports regularly, and remove permissions that are never used
code: + monthly: access-report --unused report-service -> open a ticket
options.why: Permissions drift wide over time. Regular pruning keeps a role near the least it needs.

options.label: Keep the wildcard, and add a deny for deleting backups
options.why: It blocks one bad thing and leaves every other one open: reading every database, creating users, changing policies.

options.label: Keep the wildcard, but only from the office network address
options.why: The credential leaked from inside your own logs. Network limits do not fix what the role is allowed to do.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: The job needs to read one bucket. If its credential leaks, the attacker gets the whole account.

label: Send this request: it breaks it
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: The credential listed every database and deleted the backups, because the role was allowed to do anything to anything. The job only ever read one bucket.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: A report job that could burn the account down
body: The credential listed every database and deleted the backups, because the role was allowed to do anything to anything. The job only ever read one bucket.
The access report even said so: "Permissions granted: everything".
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

label: Untick this one, it does not fix the cause
Pick this change
Picked everything that fixes it? Apply the patch
Open the Fix tab

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: The role reads one bucket and nothing else, and its credential comes from a role that expires within the hour. A regular look at what is actually used stops it creeping back to a wildcard.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: The least it needs, for the least time
body: The role reads one bucket and nothing else, and its credential comes from a role that expires within the hour. A regular look at what is actually used stops it creeping back to a wildcard.
Least privilege is what makes a leak an incident instead of a disaster.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: Denying deletion of backups, or limiting the network, leaves a role that can still read every database, create users and change policies. Deny lists are always one action short.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: One door shut, the rest wide open
body: Denying deletion of backups, or limiting the network, leaves a role that can still read every database, create users and change policies. Deny lists are always one action short.
Allow only what the job needs.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
